options.label: Don't use periods
options.rule: Don't use periods for academic degrees. Examples: PhD; MS.

options.label: Use periods
options.rule: Use periods for academic degrees. Examples: Ph.D.; M.S.

rules.title: Uppercase abbreviations
rules.rule: Don't use periods for uppercase abbreviations. Examples: USA; LGBT.

rules.title: Latin abbreviations
rules.rule: Don't use Latin abbreviations such as i.e., ibid., or etc.

options.label: BC and AD
options.rule: Use BC and AD for year notations when specified. Examples: 400 BC; AD 2025.

options.label: BCE and CE
options.rule: Use BCE and CE for year notations when specified. Examples: 400 BCE; 2025 CE.

options.label: DD/MM/YYYY
options.description: Include zeros for single-digit days and months.
options.rule: Write dates as DD/MM/YYYY, including zeros for single-digit days and months.

options.label: Write out, starting with date
options.rule: Write out dates starting with the day. Example: 13 December 2024.

options.label: MM/DD/YYYY
options.description: Include zeros for single-digit days and months.
options.rule: Write dates as MM/DD/YYYY, including zeros for single-digit days and months.

options.label: Write out, starting with month
options.rule: Write out dates starting with the month. Example: December 13, 2024.

options.label: YYYY-MM-DD
options.description: Include zeros for single-digit days and months.
options.rule: Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD, including zeros for single-digit days and months.

options.label: 12-hour with a.m./p.m.
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and a.m./p.m.

options.label: 12-hour with a.m./p.m. and noon/midnight
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and a.m./p.m. Use the words noon and midnight rather than 12:00 p.m. and 12:00 a.m. respectively.

options.label: 12-hour with am/pm
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and am/pm.

options.label: 12-hour with am/pm and noon/midnight
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and am/pm. Use the words noon and midnight rather than 12:00 pm and 12:00 am respectively.

options.label: 12-hour with A.M./P.M.
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and A.M./P.M.

options.label: 12-hour with A.M./P.M. and noon/midnight
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and A.M./P.M. Use the words noon and midnight rather than 12:00 P.M. and 12:00 A.M. respectively.

options.label: 12-hour with AM/PM
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and AM/PM.

options.label: 12-hour with AM/PM and "noon"/"midnight"
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 12-hour clock and AM/PM. Use the words "noon" and "midnight" rather than 12:00 PM and 12:00 AM respectively.

options.label: 24-hour clock
options.rule: When writing about times of the day, use the 24-hour clock.

options.label: Place the domain in parentheses
options.rule: When writing email addresses, place the domain in parentheses. Example: username@(domain.com).

options.label: Replace @ with [at] and periods with [dot]
options.rule: When writing email addresses, replace @ with "at" in brackets and periods with "dot" in brackets. Example: firstname[dot]lastname[at]domain[dot]com.

options.label: Replace @ with [at] and spaces
options.rule: When writing email addresses, replace @ with "at" in brackets with a space on either side. Example: username [at] domain.com.

options.label: Replace @ with at and spaces
options.rule: When writing email addresses, replace @ with "at" with a space on either side. Example: username at domain.com.

options.label: Use the standard format
options.rule: When writing email addresses, use the standard format. Example: username@domain.com.

options.label: Use 00 for the country code
options.rule: For country codes in phone numbers, use 00 for the country code. Examples: 0044; 001.

options.label: Use + for the country code
options.rule: For country codes in phone numbers, use + for the country code. Examples: +44; +1.

rules.title: Writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP)

options.label: No spaces or special characters
options.rule: When writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), do not use any spaces or special characters between the digits. Example: +11234567890.

options.label: Use hyphens
options.rule: When writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), use hyphens to separate the country code, the area code, the local prefix, and the last four digits. Example: +1-123-456-7890.

options.label: Use periods
options.rule: When writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), use periods to separate the country code, the area code, the local prefix, and the last four digits. Example: +1.123.456.7890.

options.label: Use spaces
options.rule: When writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), use spaces to separate the country code, the area code, the local prefix, and the last four digits. Example: +1 123 456 7890.

options.label: Area code in parentheses, no country code
options.rule: When writing phone numbers that use the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), do not include the country code, place the area code in parentheses followed by a space, and use a hyphen between the local prefix and the last four digits. Example: (123) 456-7890.

rules.title: Decimal numbers of less than 1
rules.rule: For decimal numbers of less than 1, always use a 0 before the decimal point.

options.label: Use a multiplication sign, with spaces
options.rule: For two-dimensional and three-dimensional measurements, use a multiplication sign between the numerals, with spaces. Examples: 1200 × 1800; 13 × 7.5 × 4.

options.label: Use a multiplication sign, without spaces
options.rule: For two-dimensional and three-dimensional measurements, use a multiplication sign between the numerals, without spaces. Examples: 1200×1800; 13×7.5×4.

options.label: Use a lowercase x, with spaces
options.rule: For two-dimensional and three-dimensional measurements, use a lowercase letter "x," with spaces. Examples: 1200 x 1800; 13 x 7.5 x 4.

options.label: Use a lowercase x, without spaces
options.rule: For two-dimensional and three-dimensional measurements, use a lowercase letter "x," without spaces. Examples: 1200x1800; 13x7.5x4.

rules.title: Spacing in mathematical expressions or equations
rules.rule: Between elements in a mathematical expression or equation, use spaces. Examples: 7x − 5; a + b = c.

rules.title: When referring to a symbol
rules.rule: When referring to a symbol, spell out the name, followed by the symbol in parentheses. Examples: The equal sign (=) is used in mathematical equations; a period (.) is also called a full stop (.).

options.label: Abbreviate with a numeral, spell out without
options.rule: For units of measure, abbreviate when used with a numeral but spell out when used without. Examples: Several kilometers away; 7 km.

options.label: Always abbreviate
options.rule: For units of measure, always abbreviate, with or without a numeral.

options.label: Always spell out
options.rule: For units of measure, always spell out, with or without a numeral. Examples: Several kilometers away; 7 kilometers.

options.label: Use commas
options.rule: Use commas to separate large numbers into units of three. Example: 10,000,000.

options.label: Use spaces
options.rule: Use spaces to separate large numbers into units of three. Example: 10 000 000.

options.label: Don't use a space
options.rule: For measurements, do not use a space between a numeral and unit. Examples: 10MB; 5kg.

options.label: Use a space
options.rule: For measurements, use a space between a numeral and unit. Examples: 10 MB; 5 kg.

rules.title: When ampersands are part of a common abbreviation

options.label: Don't use spaces
options.rule: When ampersands are part of a common abbreviation, do not use spaces. Examples: R&D; M&A.

options.label: Use spaces
options.rule: When ampersands are part of a common abbreviation, use spaces. Examples: R & D; M & A.

rules.title: Replacing ampersands in running text
rules.rule: Replace & with "and," except in company names, common abbreviations, titles, software code, and mathematical equations. Example: We’re increasing the budget for multiple departments, including R&D and Sales.

options.label: Spell out the word after the amount
options.rule: When writing currencies, spell out the word after the amount. Examples: 100 dollars; 100 euros.

options.label: Use the symbol before the amount, no space
options.rule: When writing currencies, use the currency symbol before the amount, without a space. Examples: $100; €100.

options.label: Use the symbol before the amount, with a space
options.rule: When writing currencies, use the currency symbol before the amount, with a space. Examples: $ 100; € 100.

options.label: Use the ISO code before the amount
options.rule: When writing currencies, use the ISO code before the amount, with a space. Examples: USD 100; EUR 100.

options.label: Use m and bn, without a space
options.rule: When writing large sums of money, use "m" and "bn" instead of "million" and "billion," without a space. Examples: EUR 100m; USD 500bn.

options.label: Use mn and bn, with a space
options.rule: When writing large sums of money, use "mn" and "bn" instead of "million" and "billion," with a space. Examples: EUR 100 mn; USD 500 bn.

options.label: Spell out million and billion
options.rule: When writing large sums of money, spell out the words "million" and "billion." Examples: EUR 100 million; USD 500 billion.

options.label: Use % without a space
options.rule: When writing percentages, use % without a space. Example: 99%.

options.label: Use % with a space
options.rule: When writing percentages, use % with a space. Example: 99 %.

options.label: Use per cent
options.rule: When writing percentages, use "per cent." Example: 99 per cent.

options.label: Use percent
options.rule: When writing percentages, use "percent." Example: 99 percent.

options.label: Use numerals and spell out the unit
options.rule: When writing temperatures, use numerals for the measurement, but spell out the full unit. Examples: 32 degrees Celsius; 273.16 kelvins.

options.label: Use the unit symbol, with a space
options.rule: When writing temperatures, use numerals followed by the unit symbol, with a space. Examples: 32 ºC; 273.16 K.

options.label: Use the unit symbol, without a space
options.rule: When writing temperatures, use numerals followed by the unit symbol, without a space. Examples: 32ºC; 273.16K.

rules.title: Comma after i.e. and e.g. in text

options.label: Don't use
examples: All attendees (i.e. registered participants) will receive a badge.
options.rule: Do not use a comma after i.e. and e.g. in text. Example: All attendees (i.e. registered participants) will receive a badge.

options.label: Use
examples: All attendees (i.e., registered participants) will receive a badge.
options.rule: Use a comma after i.e. and e.g. in text. Example: All attendees (i.e., registered participants) will receive a badge.

rules.title: Comma after a short introductory phrase

options.label: Don't use a comma
examples: At work employees are required to wear safety gear.
options.rule: Do not use a comma after a short introductory phrase. Example: At work employees are required to wear safety gear.

options.label: Use a comma
examples: At work, employees are required to wear safety gear.
options.rule: Use a comma after a short introductory phrase. Example: At work, employees are required to wear safety gear.

options.label: Don't use
options.rule: Do not use serial commas. Example: Apples, oranges and bananas.

options.label: Use
options.rule: Use serial commas. Example: Apples, oranges, and bananas.

options.label: Use the ellipsis character
options.rule: For an ellipsis, use the ellipsis character. Example: …

options.label: Use three spaced periods
options.rule: For an ellipsis, use three spaced periods. Example: . . .

rules.title: Exclamation marks
rules.rule: Do not use exclamation marks.

rules.title: Using the plus sign to mean and
rules.rule: Do not use the plus sign to mean "and," unless it is part of a proper noun.

options.label: Use a colon (formal)
options.rule: After a salutation, use a colon in formal contexts. Example: Dear Mr. Smith:

options.label: Use a comma (informal)
options.rule: After a salutation, use a comma in informal contexts. Example: Dear John,

rules.title: Using a slash to mean or
rules.rule: Do not use a slash to mean "or."

rules.title: Curly or straight quotation marks and apostrophes

options.label: Curly
options.rule: Use curly quotation marks and apostrophes. Example: “The king’s hat”.

options.label: Straight
options.rule: Use straight quotation marks and apostrophes. Example: "The king's hat".

options.label: Double primary, single secondary (American English)
examples: “The first chapter of the UN Charter ‘Purposes and Principles’ is crucial,” said the professor.
options.rule: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and single quotation marks for secondary quotations, following American English style. Example: “The first chapter of the UN Charter ‘Purposes and Principles’ is crucial,” said the professor.

options.label: Single primary, double secondary (British English)
examples: ‘The first chapter of the UN Charter “Purposes and Principles” is crucial’, said the professor.
options.rule: Use single quotation marks for primary quotations and double quotation marks for secondary quotations, following British English style. Example: ‘The first chapter of the UN Charter “Purposes and Principles” is crucial’, said the professor.

rules.title: When indicating a range of numbers or dates

options.label: En dash without spaces
options.rule: When indicating a range of numbers or dates, use an en dash without spaces. Examples: Monday–Saturday; 2001–2003.

options.label: Use the word to
options.rule: When indicating a range of numbers or dates, use the word "to." Examples: Monday to Saturday; 2001 to 2003.

options.label: Hyphen with spaces
options.rule: When indicating a range of numbers or dates, use a hyphen with spaces. Examples: Monday - Saturday; 2001 - 2003.

options.label: Hyphen without spaces
options.rule: When indicating a range of numbers or dates, use a hyphen without spaces. Examples: Monday-Saturday; 2001-2003.

options.label: Em dash with spaces
options.rule: Use an em dash with spaces. Example: I’m here — finally.

options.label: Em dash without spaces
options.rule: Use an em dash without spaces. Example: I’m here—finally.

options.label: En dash with spaces
options.rule: Use an en dash with spaces. Example: I’m here – finally.

rules.title: Active and passive voice
rules.rule: Use active voice. Use passive voice only when the subject is unknown or irrelevant.

options.label: Don't use
examples: We will do our best to get back to you, but we cannot guarantee a response.
options.rule: Do not use contractions. Example: We will do our best to get back to you, but we cannot guarantee a response.

options.label: Use
examples: We’ll do our best to get back to you, but we can’t guarantee a response.
options.rule: Use contractions. Example: We’ll do our best to get back to you, but we can’t guarantee a response.

options.label: Use, but avoid negative contractions
examples: We’ll do our best to get back to you, but we cannot guarantee a response.
options.rule: Use contractions, but avoid negative contractions. Example: We’ll do our best to get back to you, but we cannot guarantee a response.

options.label: Don't make changes to quoted material
options.rule: Do not make changes to quoted material, regardless of style rules.

options.label: Edit quoted material to adhere to style rules
options.rule: Edit quoted material to adhere to style rules.

rules.title: Capitalization
rules.rule: Do not use all caps, except when writing out an acronym, initialism, or proper noun. Example: NASA is a US government agency.

rules.title: Inclusive language
rules.rule: Replace binary representations of gender with gender-neutral language.

rules.title: Directional language and visual cues
rules.rule: Do not use directional language, or words that depend on visual cues, such as "here" or "below."

rules.title: Idioms, colloquialisms, and culture-specific phrases
rules.rule: Do not use idioms, colloquialisms, or words or phrases specific to a particular culture.

rules.title: Imperative mood in instructions
rules.rule: When writing instructions, use the imperative mood.

options.label: Don't use first- and second-person pronouns
examples: The talent acquisition specialist will contact candidates by Friday.
options.rule: Do not use first- and second-person pronouns, for a more impersonal tone. Example: The talent acquisition specialist will contact candidates by Friday.

options.label: Use first- and second-person pronouns where appropriate
options.rule: Use first- and second-person pronouns where appropriate, for a more personal tone. Example: We'll contact you by Friday.

rules.title: Positive language
rules.rule: Use positive language.

rules.title: Required actions
rules.rule: Use "must" when an action is required, rather than "have to," "should," or other alternatives. Example: You must log in to view this page.

rules.title: References to the existing text
rules.rule: Do not use phrases that refer to the existing text when using them would be redundant.

rules.title: Redundant phrases
rules.rule: Do not use redundant phrases where the same meaning is repeated in a single phrase. Examples: Added bonus; basic fundamentals.

rules.title: Shorter words
rules.rule: When there is a shorter word available, use it over the longer word when appropriate.
